procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated September 9, 1950, passed by the Presidency Magistrate of Bombay, discharging the appellants (accused 1 and 2) from facing trial in the Court of Session on a charge under s. 409, Indian Penal Code.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Bombay High Court, in Criminal Revision Application No. 1425 of 1951, set aside the order of the Presidency Magistrate on June 22, 1951. The High Court directed that the appellants be committed to the Court of Session, the first appellant for a charge under s. 409, Indian Penal Code, and the second appellant under s. 409 read with s. 109, Indian Penal Code, based on the charges framed by the High Court's Division Bench on March 1, 1950, during a previous hearing.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The accused persons (appellants) moved the Supreme Court and obtained special leave to appeal the High Court's order directing their committal to the Court of Session. Special leave was granted on January 15, 1952, and further proceedings against the appellants in the Court of Session were stayed.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court has the jurisdiction to revise an order of discharge passed by a Presidency Magistrate.

facts: A Presidency Magistrate of Bombay passed an order discharging the appellants.
The Bombay High Court, in revision, set aside the discharge order and directed that the appellants be committed to the Court of Session for trial.
The appellants appealed to the Supreme Court, arguing that the High Court had no jurisdiction to revise a discharge order passed by a Presidency Magistrate.
law: Section 435 of the Code of Criminal Procedure allows the High Court to call for and examine the record of any proceeding before any inferior criminal court.
Section 439 of the Code grants the High Court, in revision, all the powers of an Appellate Court under Section 423, and these powers can be exercised in the case of 'any proceeding'.

Section 441 of the Code specifically provides a procedure for when the High Court calls for the record of a proceeding from a Presidency Magistrate, allowing the magistrate to submit a statement of reasons for their decision.
application: The Court first established that a Presidency Magistrate's court is an 'inferior criminal court' under Section 435, meaning the High Court is authorized to call for and examine its records.

The Court rejected the appellants' argument that the High Court can only revise orders that are appealable. It held that Section 439 is worded in very wide terms, applying to 'any proceeding', not just appeals. Therefore, the non-appealable nature of a discharge order does not prevent the High Court from revising it.

The Court pointed to Section 441 as further proof of the High Court's jurisdiction. This section, which specifically deals with proceedings from a Presidency Magistrate, would be pointless if the High Court had no power to overrule or set aside the magistrate's order. The existence of this provision demonstrates the Legislature's intent to allow for such revision.
By reading these sections together, the Court found a clear basis for the High Court's power to review and, if necessary, set aside a discharge order from a Presidency Magistrate.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellants' challenge and affirmed the High Court's jurisdiction. It held that under the combined reading of Sections 435, 439, and 441 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the High Court has ample power to revise an order of discharge passed by a Presidency Magistrate and to direct the committal of the accused to the Court of Session.

issue.issue_text: Whether the inordinate delay in bringing the accused to trial, for which they were primarily responsible, could be a ground for not holding the trial.

facts: There was an inordinate delay in bringing the case to trial, with the case pending for over nine years after the charge-sheet was submitted.
The appellants (the accused) argued that due to this long delay, the trial should not be held.
The Court found that the accused persons themselves had "largely contributed" to this delay and were "primarily responsible" for it.
application: The Court reasoned that since the appellants were themselves primarily responsible for the delay, they could not be allowed to make a grievance of it.
The Court stated that the appellants had "largely to thank themselves for this result" and therefore had no "just grievance" regarding the pending case.
Because the blame for the delay did not lie solely with the prosecution but significantly with the accused, the Court refused to entertain the plea that the trial should not proceed.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellants' contention, holding that the inordinate delay in bringing them to trial could not be a ground for not holding the trial, as they themselves were primarily responsible for causing that delay.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court's power under Section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to order a committal for trial is restricted to cases involving an appeal from an order of acquittal.

law.fact: Section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure grants the High Court revisional jurisdiction over proceedings in lower criminal courts.
Section 439 allows the High Court, in its revisional capacity, to exercise any of the powers conferred on an appellate court by Section 423.
The power to order that an accused be committed for trial is contained in Section 423(1)(a).
Section 423(1)(a) begins with the phrase "in an appeal from an order of acquittal".

application.fact: The Court rejected the argument that the High Court's power to order a committal is restricted to cases where there is an appeal from an order of acquittal.
The Court identified the core fallacy in this argument as wrongly reading all the words of Section 423 (including the conditional phrase "in an appeal from an order of acquittal") into Section 439.
The Court clarified that Section 439 only incorporates the *powers* contained in Section 423, not the *cases* or *circumstances* in which an appellate court would exercise them.

The scope for exercising these powers is determined by Section 439 itself, which contains the "sweeping provision" that the High Court may act "in the case of any proceeding" that comes before it for revision.

Therefore, the Court must look to Section 423 to find out the *nature* of the power it can exercise (e.g., ordering a committal), but it looks to Section 439 to determine the *cases* in which it can exercise that power (i.e., in any proceeding under its revisional jurisdiction).

The Court also reasoned that if the appellant's argument were accepted, Section 439 would become redundant in this respect, as appeals against acquittal are already specifically dealt with under other sections of the Code.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court's power under Section 439 to order a committal for trial is not restricted to cases involving an appeal from an order of acquittal. The High Court can exercise this power, which is borrowed from Section 423, in any proceeding that is properly before it under its broad revisional jurisdiction.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court erred in setting aside the magistrate's order of discharge, which was based on the finding that there were no 'sufficient grounds' for committal.

facts: A Presidency Magistrate conducted a commitment proceeding and considered a large volume of evidence from both the prosecution and the defense.
The magistrate concluded that "no criminal court would convict the accused" on the evidence presented and that a conviction was not "reasonably probable."
Based on this finding, the magistrate discharged the accused, holding there were not "sufficient grounds for committing the accused for trial."
The High Court, exercising its revisional powers, set aside the magistrate's order of discharge and directed that the accused be committed to the Court of Session for trial.
The High Court found that the evidence made out a prima facie case and could be reasonably relied upon.
law: The central legal question revolves around the interpretation of "sufficient grounds" for committal under the Code of Criminal Procedure (ss. 209, 210, 213).
The Supreme Court clarified the duty of a committing magistrate: the magistrate should not weigh the evidence to determine if a conviction is probable or bound to follow.
The correct test is whether there is "credible evidence which, if accepted, may lead to conviction."
A magistrate should only discharge the accused if they conclude that "the evidence is such that no Court would ever convict."
If there is evidence for and against the accused, the magistrate's duty is to commit the case for trial, not to discharge.
application: The Supreme Court found that the magistrate had applied the wrong legal test. By conducting an elaborate evaluation of the evidence to determine the probability of a conviction, the magistrate acted as if he were the trial court, which exceeded his role in a commitment proceeding.
The magistrate's reasoning that he should not commit unless a conviction was "reasonably probable" was incorrect.
The High Court, in contrast, correctly assessed the situation. It found that a prima facie case had been made out and that the evidence was not such that it could be dismissed as wholly unreliable.
The Supreme Court agreed with the High Court's assessment, stating that this was "pre-eminently a case for committal to the Court of Session."
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appeal, holding that the High Court did not err. The magistrate's order of discharge was deemed "highly improper" because he had applied the wrong standard by weighing the evidence to assess the probability of conviction, instead of simply determining if there were sufficient grounds (i.e., credible evidence that could potentially lead to a conviction) to send the case to trial. Therefore, the High Court's order setting aside the discharge and directing committal was affirmed.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court has the jurisdiction to revise an order of discharge passed by a Presidency Magistrate.
appellant_arguments: The appellants contended that the High Court did not have the necessary jurisdiction to revise the order of discharge passed by the Presidency Magistrate.
respondent_arguments: The respondent (the State) argued that the High Court possessed the jurisdiction to revise the magistrate's order of discharge.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the inordinate delay in bringing the accused to trial, for which they were primarily responsible, could be a ground for not holding the trial.
appellant_arguments: The trial should not proceed due to the inordinate delay of more than nine years since the charge-sheet was submitted.
respondent_arguments: The appellants themselves are largely responsible for the delay and therefore have no just grievance.
The delay should not be a reason to prevent the case from proceeding to trial.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court's power under Section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to order a committal for trial is restricted to cases involving an appeal from an order of acquittal.
appellant_arguments: The appellants' legal arguments implied that the High Court's power to order a committal did not extend to revising an order of discharge in this manner, suggesting its powers were more restricted.
respondent_arguments: The respondent (the State) argued that the High Court's powers were broad enough to set aside the discharge and order a committal for trial.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court erred in setting aside the magistrate's order of discharge, which was based on the finding that there were no 'sufficient grounds' for committal.
appellant_arguments: The magistrate correctly discharged the accused after a full and elaborate consideration of evidence from both prosecution and defence.
The transactions alleged to be fictitious were real, had innocent explanations, and were properly recorded in the company's books.
The magistrate was correct in finding that no criminal court would convict the accused on the available evidence.
respondent_arguments: The magistrate erred in discharging the accused, as there was a prima facie case.
The magnitude of the case and the potential punishment justified a committal to the Court of Session.
Given the mass of circumstances and evidence, it cannot be said that no court would ever convict the accused.

cases.principle: Cited as a case that correctly laid down the legal position regarding the scope of a magistrate's inquiry in committal proceedings.

cases.case_name: A Division Bench case of the Bombay High Court
cases.principle: The words 'sufficient grounds for committing', do not mean sufficient grounds for convicting.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A committing magistrate ought to commit a party for trial when the evidence is sufficient to put them on trial. Such a case arises when credible witnesses make statements that, if believed, would sustain a conviction. The function of weighing testimony, including considering improbabilities and apparent discrepancies, belongs to the trial court, not the committing magistrate.
obiter: It is inexpedient for an appellate court to express any opinion on controversial matters of fact when directing a committal for trial, as such observations may prejudice either party.
Both the courts below have travelled beyond the limits proper for decision at the stage at which the case was before them.
The accused persons did not consult their best interests when they invited the courts below to go into those questions which did not properly arise for determination at that stage.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The role of a committing magistrate is not to conduct a detailed examination of evidence to determine which side's version is more acceptable, as that is the function of the trial court. The magistrate's duty is limited to determining if there are 'sufficient grounds' for committal, which means assessing whether a prima facie case exists based on evidence that is not so incredible that no reasonable court could ever convict upon it. In this case, the magistrate overstepped by weighing the voluminous evidence and discharging the accused, when it was not possible to say that no court would ever convict them.
legal_tests_applied: The test for a magistrate considering committal is whether a prima facie case is made out against the accused by the evidence of witnesses entitled to a reasonable degree of credit.
The expression 'sufficient grounds' for committal means that a magistrate should not discharge the accused unless the evidence 'cannot possibly justify a conviction'.

Applying the test to the facts, the question is: 'can it be said that there is no evidence to make out a prima facie case, or that the voluminous evidence adduced in this case is so incredible that no reasonable body of persons could rely upon it?'
why_appellant_lost: The appellants could not complain about the inordinate delay in the trial because they themselves were primarily responsible for it, and such delay is not a ground for preventing the trial from proceeding.

The court rejected the contention that the High Court lacked jurisdiction to revise an order of discharge passed by a Presidency Magistrate, holding that the High Court did have the necessary jurisdiction.

The magistrate erred by travelling beyond the proper scope of a committal proceeding. He 'embarked upon a very detailed exaimnation of the evidence in the case, to find which version is the more acceptable one' instead of merely determining if a prima facie case existed.

Given the 'mass of circumstances and evidence in the case it is not possible to say that no Court would ever convict the accused or that the Judge would withdraw the case', therefore the magistrate's finding to the contrary was incorrect.
why_respondent_won: The High Court correctly exercised its jurisdiction in revising the magistrate's order of discharge.
The delay in proceedings, having been caused by the appellants, could not be used as a reason to quash the trial.
The evidence on record was sufficient to establish a prima facie case for committal, as it could not be said that the evidence was so incredible that no reasonable court could rely on it.
The High Court was correct in its view that 'the magnitude of the case and the amount of punishment in the event of a conviction, clearly justified a committal.'
policy_considerations: The court emphasized the distinct roles of the committing court and the trial court, noting that both lower courts 'have travelled beyond the limits proper for decision at the stagi:! 1lt which the case was before them.'

The court expressed a desire for the trial to proceed without further delay: 'It is hoped that the Court of Session, which will now be in seizin of the case, will conduct the trial and conclude the proceedings with all reasonable speed and without any avoidable delay.'

To ensure a fair trial, the court deliberately avoided expressing its own opinion on the merits of the factual controversies, stating, 'We do not think it desirable that any observations made by us, should prejudice either party at the trial.'
